Conditions that affect breathing.Appendicitis: Appendicitis is inflammation of the appendix, in the lower right abdomen.
Conditions that affect breathing.Dermatitis: Dermatitis is skin inflammation, such as eczema or contact rashes.
Conditions that affect breathing.Gout: Gout is a joint problem caused by uric acid crystals.
Conditions that affect breathing.Cataract: A cataract clouds the eye's lens and has nothing to do with breathing, though it's very common in older adults.
Conditions that affect breathing.Shingles: Shingles is a painful rash caused by the chickenpox virus waking up in nerves, not a breathing issue.
Conditions that affect breathing.Bunions: Bunions are bony bumps on the foot beside the big toe.
Conditions that affect breathing.Diabetes: Diabetes disrupts blood sugar control, though it isn't a breathing condition itself.
Conditions that affect breathing.Tinnitus: Tinnitus is ringing in the ears, nothing to do with the lungs.

Things that protect your skin from the s.Sunscreen: SPF measures protection against UVB burning rays only; look for broad spectrum on the label to also block the UVA rays that age skin.
Things that protect your skin from the s.Sun hat: A hat with a brim of at least three inches shades the face, ears and neck, where skin cancers often appear.
Things that protect your skin from the s.Parasol: Parasols were status symbols in ancient China and Egypt, where shade meant you did not have to labor outdoors.
Things that protect your skin from the s.Rash guard: Rash guards were first made for surfers to prevent board rash, and their tight weave happens to block most UV rays too.
Things that protect your skin from the s.Zinc cream: Zinc oxide is a mineral that sits on the skin and reflects light, and the colorful zinc stripes of 1980s lifeguards were its comeback.
Things that protect your skin from the s.Long sleeves: Loose long sleeves can protect skin better than sunscreen, as long as the fabric is tightly woven; thin white cotton can let UV through.
Things that protect your skin from the s.Beach umbrella: An umbrella cuts UV exposure but not completely, since sand and water reflect rays back up at you from below.
Things that protect your skin from the s.SPF lip balm: Lips have almost no melanin and are prone to sunburn, so lip balm with SPF is a key spot people often forget.
Things that protect your skin from the s.UPF shirt: UPF is the fabric version of SPF, and UPF 50 clothing blocks about 98 percent of the sun's UV radiation.
Things that protect your skin from the s.Sunshade: Even in shade, you can still burn: reflected and scattered UV means shade reduces exposure but never removes it.
Things that protect your skin from the s.Tanning oil: Tanning oil attracts sunlight rather than blocking it, and most contain little or no SPF, so it speeds up burning.
Things that protect your skin from the s.Baby oil: Baby oil provides no UV protection at all, and slathering it on your skin can actually help the sun cook you faster.
Things that protect your skin from the s.Bikini: The bikini is named after Bikini Atoll, where atomic bomb tests took place in 1946, chosen for its explosive effect, not for sun protection.
Things that protect your skin from the s.Flip-flops: Flip-flops cover almost none of your foot, and the tops of feet are a common spot for nasty sunburns.
Things that protect your skin from the s.Snorkel: A snorkel lets you stay face down for hours, which means your back and the backs of your legs get blasted by the sun.
Things that protect your skin from the s.Sandcastle: Competitive sand sculptors use fine clay-rich sand and packed water to make castles that stand as tall as 10 meters.
Things that protect your skin from the s.Sunbed: Sunbeds emit concentrated UV, and the World Health Organization lists them as carcinogenic to humans, so they are the opposite of protection.
Things that protect your skin from the s.Beach ball: Beach balls are fun, but they do nothing to stop UV rays, and chasing one around leaves you out in the open sun.
Things that protect your skin from the s.Lemonade: Lemonade quenches thirst but does nothing for skin; lemon juice on skin can even cause a rash when sunlight hits it.
Things that protect your skin from the s.Glitter: Glitter reflects light but gives zero UV protection, and body glitter has been banned on some festival grounds as microplastic.
Things that protect your skin from the s.Tank top: A tank top leaves shoulders bare, which is exactly where people burn most, so it is a trap rather than protection.
Things that protect your skin from the s.Frisbee: The Frisbee got its name from the Frisbie Baking Company pie tins that college students tossed around in the 1940s.
Things that protect your skin from the s.Tan accelerator: Tan accelerators promise to speed up tanning, but a tan is itself a sign of skin damage, so they do not protect you.
Things that protect your skin from the s.Ice pop: Ice pops cool you down and are fun at the beach, but they cannot shield your skin, and popsicles were invented by an 11-year-old by accident.

Diseases you can be vaccinated against.Measles: Measles is among the most contagious diseases known, and one case can infect about 12 to 18 unvaccinated people nearby.
Diseases you can be vaccinated against.Polio: Polio has been cut by over 99 percent since 1988 thanks to vaccines, and it remains endemic in just a few countries.
Diseases you can be vaccinated against.Mumps: Mumps causes swollen cheeks and was common until a vaccine arrived in the 1960s, which was developed from a sample of the developer's daughter.
Diseases you can be vaccinated against.Tetanus: Tetanus is caused by bacteria in soil entering wounds, not by rust itself, and boosters are recommended about every ten years.
Diseases you can be vaccinated against.Flu: Flu viruses mutate constantly, which is why the vaccine is updated every year and why a new shot is needed.
Diseases you can be vaccinated against.Chickenpox: Chickenpox has a vaccine since 1995, and the virus can later reawaken in adults as shingles.
Diseases you can be vaccinated against.Whooping cough: Whooping cough is named for the whoop sound of an inhaled breath after coughing, and it is also called pertussis.
Diseases you can be vaccinated against.Hepatitis B: Hepatitis B vaccine, first available in 1981, was the first vaccine against a human cancer, since it prevents liver cancer.
Diseases you can be vaccinated against.Rabies: Rabies is almost always fatal once symptoms start, but vaccination right after a bite prevents it; Pasteur gave the first one in 1885.
Diseases you can be vaccinated against.Smallpox: Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 and is the only human disease to have been wiped out by vaccination.
Diseases you can be vaccinated against.Shingles: Shingles is the chickenpox virus reactivating years later, and a vaccine is recommended for older adults.
Diseases you can be vaccinated against.HPV: The HPV vaccine protects against the virus behind most cervical cancers and is among the first vaccines to prevent a cancer.
Diseases you can be vaccinated against.Diphtheria: Diphtheria was once a leading cause of child death, and in 1925 a sled-dog relay raced its antitoxin to Nome, Alaska.
Diseases you can be vaccinated against.Yellow fever: Yellow fever, spread by mosquitoes, has a vaccine that gives lifelong protection after a single dose.
Diseases you can be vaccinated against.Common cold: The common cold is caused by hundreds of different viruses, mostly rhinoviruses, which is why no vaccine exists.
Diseases you can be vaccinated against.Asthma: Asthma is a chronic airway condition that cannot be prevented by vaccine, though flu shots help avoid attacks.
Diseases you can be vaccinated against.Diabetes: Diabetes is a metabolic disease, not an infection, so no vaccine prevents it, and insulin was discovered in 1921.
Diseases you can be vaccinated against.Hay fever: Hay fever is an allergy to pollen and not a fever, and it is not caused by hay, so a vaccine will not stop it.
Diseases you can be vaccinated against.Strep throat: Strep throat is a bacterial infection, and there is currently no vaccine for it, only antibiotics.
Diseases you can be vaccinated against.Sunburn: Sunburn is skin damage from UV light, not an infection, so only sunscreen and shade protect you.
Diseases you can be vaccinated against.Migraine: Migraine is a neurological condition, not an infection, and about one in seven people worldwide are affected.
Diseases you can be vaccinated against.Acne: Acne is linked to hormones, oil and bacteria, but it is not preventable by vaccine.
Diseases you can be vaccinated against.Head lice: Head lice are tiny insects that spread through contact, so no vaccine exists, and they prefer clean hair.
Diseases you can be vaccinated against.Athlete's foot: Athlete's foot is a fungal infection, and no vaccine exists, while the fungus likes damp locker rooms.

Things you'd see on a construction site.Crane: A tower crane is built up piece by piece, and it can climb the building it's helping to construct.
Things you'd see on a construction site.Hard hat: Hard hats came into use in the early 1900s, and the first ones were made from canvas and glue.
Things you'd see on a construction site.Scaffolding: Scaffolding in some Asian countries, like Hong Kong, is still built from bamboo, even for skyscrapers.
Things you'd see on a construction site.Bulldozer: A bulldozer is a tractor with a blade, and its name is a mystery, though possibly from the 1880s.
Things you'd see on a construction site.Cement mixer: A cement mixer drum rotates continually, to keep concrete from setting before it's poured.
Things you'd see on a construction site.Excavator: An excavator can swing its cab a full circle, and its arm can dig deeper than most backhoes.
Things you'd see on a construction site.Rebar: Rebar is steel bar embedded in concrete, because concrete is strong under compression but weak when stretched.
Things you'd see on a construction site.Wheelbarrow: A wheelbarrow was invented in China around 2,000 years ago, and some early ones had a sail.
Things you'd see on a construction site.Hi-vis vest: Hi-vis vests help drivers spot workers, and they use fluorescent fabric with reflective stripes.
Things you'd see on a construction site.Jackhammer: A jackhammer uses compressed air to hammer a chisel thousands of times per minute.
Things you'd see on a construction site.Traffic cone: Traffic cones were invented in 1940 by Charles Rudabaker, and they're typically orange for visibility.
Things you'd see on a construction site.Dump truck: A dump truck tilts its bed using hydraulics, and the largest mining ones can carry hundreds of tons.
Things you'd see on a construction site.Forklift: A forklift uses a counterweight at the rear, to keep it from tipping over with a heavy load.
Things you'd see on a construction site.Stethoscope: A stethoscope is a doctor's listening tool, which has nothing to do with a building site, though both involve plenty of noise.
Things you'd see on a construction site.Easel: An easel holds a painter's canvas upright, a studio item rather than something you would haul onto a muddy worksite.
Things you'd see on a construction site.Chef's hat: A chef's hat, or toque, has traditionally got pleats, and legend says 100 stand for ways to cook an egg.
Things you'd see on a construction site.Gavel: A gavel is the small mallet of a judge or auctioneer, and it signals order in a courtroom, not on a building site.
Things you'd see on a construction site.Cash register: A cash register belongs to a shop counter, and the first mechanical one was invented in 1879 to stop theft by clerks.
Things you'd see on a construction site.Treadmill: A treadmill is for exercise, found in a gym.
Things you'd see on a construction site.Ballot box: A ballot box belongs to elections, and the voting place is the place for it.
Things you'd see on a construction site.Choir robe: A choir robe belongs in a church or concert hall.
Things you'd see on a construction site.Surfboard: A surfboard belongs on the waves, and modern ones are usually foam wrapped in fiberglass resin and glass cloth.
Things you'd see on a construction site.Hospital bed: A hospital bed belongs in a hospital, and they typically adjust with a motor or crank.
Things you'd see on a construction site.Grand piano: A grand piano belongs in a concert hall or living room, and it's far too delicate for a building site.

C-suite job titles.CEO: Chief Executive Officer, the top boss who answers to the board. In US firms the CEO is typically also the public face of the company.
C-suite job titles.CFO: Chief Financial Officer, who oversees money matters from budgets to reporting. CFOs are often the second most powerful executive.
C-suite job titles.COO: Chief Operating Officer, who runs day-to-day operations. They often serve as the CEO's right hand and are common successors.
C-suite job titles.CTO: Chief Technology Officer, who sets the tech direction. In startups the CTO is often a founding engineer.
C-suite job titles.CMO: Chief Marketing Officer, in charge of brand and customer strategy. The role grew a lot with the rise of digital advertising.
C-suite job titles.CIO: Chief Information Officer, who manages a company's IT systems. It was one of the first C-suite roles beyond the classic ones.
C-suite job titles.CHRO: Chief Human Resources Officer, who leads hiring and staff policy. The title reflects HR's rise to the boardroom.
C-suite job titles.CISO: Chief Information Security Officer, responsible for defending against hackers. It's a job with famously high burnout.
C-suite job titles.CPO: Chief Product Officer, who steers what a company builds. In some firms the same abbreviation means Chief People Officer.
C-suite job titles.CPA: Certified Public Accountant, a credential, not a job title in the C-suite. Passing the exam is famously tough.
C-suite job titles.CPR: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation, an emergency technique. Chest compressions are best timed to the tempo of 'Stayin' Alive'.
C-suite job titles.CVS: An American pharmacy chain, not a title. The name began as Consumer Value Stores in 1963.
C-suite job titles.CNN: Cable News Network, launched in 1980 as the first 24-hour news channel. It's a broadcaster, not an executive.
C-suite job titles.CBS: A US broadcast network that began as Columbia Broadcasting System in 1927. Its eye logo is iconic, but it's no job.
C-suite job titles.CIA: The Central Intelligence Agency, a US spy service created in 1947. It's an agency, not an office within a company.
C-suite job titles.CDC: The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, based in Atlanta. A health agency, not an executive title.
C-suite job titles.CPU: A computer's central processing unit, its brain. It's hardware, not a manager.
C-suite job titles.VP: Vice President, a senior title but not a C-suite one. Companies can have dozens of VPs, while C-level roles are few.
C-suite job titles.MBA: Master of Business Administration, a degree many executives hold. It's an education credential, not an office.
C-suite job titles.HR: Human Resources, a department. Its head may be a CHRO, but HR itself isn't a title.
C-suite job titles.PhD: Doctor of Philosophy, an academic degree. Having one doesn't make you a C-suite exec.
C-suite job titles.LLC: Limited Liability Company, a legal structure that shields owners' personal assets. It's a business type, not a person.
C-suite job titles.IPO: Initial Public Offering, when a firm first sells shares to the public. It's an event, not a title.
C-suite job titles.FBI: The Federal Bureau of Investigation, the US domestic law enforcement agency founded in 1908. It's not a corporate role.

Things in a classroom.Whiteboard: Whiteboards replaced chalkboards in many schools from the 1990s, partly because they avoid chalk dust.
Things in a classroom.Desk: The first school desks were long shared benches, and the single-seat desk only became common in the 19th century.
Things in a classroom.Chalk: Most "chalk" today is made of gypsum, not the natural limestone chalk it was named for.
Things in a classroom.Globe: Rotating a globe is the best way to see how large Africa really is, since flat maps stretch the regions near the poles.
Things in a classroom.Textbook: A textbook is often written by committee and revised every few years, so the classroom copy may already be out of date.
Things in a classroom.Projector: Overhead projectors were once the classroom's star technology; today they have been largely replaced by digital screens.
Things in a classroom.Ruler: A ruler is the simplest measuring tool, and a standard school one marks centimeters on one edge and inches on the other.
Things in a classroom.Pencil sharpener: The modern sharpener was patented in France in the 1820s, which made pencils far easier to maintain than a knife.
Things in a classroom.Bulletin board: Cork is good for a bulletin board because it grows back, as it is harvested from the bark of a cork oak tree.
Things in a classroom.Attendance sheet: Schools take attendance every day, and in many places funding is partly tied to the numbers recorded.
Things in a classroom.Pitchfork: It's a farm tool for moving hay, and for forking hay rather than facts, it's not welcome in school.
Things in a classroom.Scalpel: Scalpels belong in surgery or biology labs, not an ordinary classroom, though dissection is taught with them in advanced classes.
Things in a classroom.Anvil: Anvils belong to the forge; they weigh as much as a person and are not a typical classroom item.
Things in a classroom.Bunk bed: Bunk beds are for dorms and sleepovers, though a classroom may have a nap mat for the youngest children.
Things in a classroom.Jail cell: A cell is a place for confinement, not learning, though teachers do sometimes assign detention.
Things in a classroom.Hot tub: Hot tubs relax people, but the classic classroom sights are rows of desks, not bubbles.
Things in a classroom.Bathtub: A bathtub is a home fixture, and a classroom would have more trouble with the plumbing than the lessons.
Things in a classroom.Car lift: A car lift sits in a garage; a vocational classroom might have one in an auto shop, but a general class would not.
Things in a classroom.Fire pole: The fire pole belongs to a fire station, and schools use fire drills with stairs instead.
Things in a classroom.Hay bale: Hay bales are for barns and fields, and while they look soft, no student wants to sit on one.
Things in a classroom.Saddle: A saddle is part of riding gear, and so belongs in stables, not classrooms.
Things in a classroom.Altar: An altar is part of a house of worship, so a standard classroom would not have one.
Things in a classroom.Slot machine: Slots are casino games; school is meant to be where odds are taught as math, not gambled.
Things in a classroom.Escalator: An escalator moves people in malls and stations, and schools mostly use plain stairs.

Construction trades.Plumber: Plumbers lay and fix pipes, and the word comes from the Latin plumbum, lead, which Romans used for water pipes.
Construction trades.Electrician: Electricians wire up buildings, and in many places they must complete an apprenticeship of several years before working alone.
Construction trades.Carpenter: Cabinetmakers build fine furniture such as chests and desks, and their craft is distinct from carpentry because the joinery must be nearly invisible.
Construction trades.Bricklayer: Bricklayers can lay hundreds of bricks in a day, and bonding patterns make walls stronger than the bricks alone.
Construction trades.Roofer: Roofers work at height, and a slate roof can last over a century if well laid.
Construction trades.Plasterer: Plasterers coat walls and ceilings with a smooth finish, a craft known since ancient Egypt.
Construction trades.Glazier: Glaziers cut and fit window glass, and the modern flat pane only became cheap after the float glass process in the 1950s.
Construction trades.Tiler: Tilers lay ceramic tiles on floors and walls, and the craft goes back to the ancient Mesopotamians.
Construction trades.Scaffolder: Scaffolders build the temporary frames that let others work at height, and some scaffolding in Asia is still made of bamboo.
Construction trades.Welder: Welders fuse metal parts with extreme heat, and look away from the arc, which can burn the eyes within moments.
Construction trades.Joiner: A joiner makes wooden items such as doors, windows and stairs, often in a workshop and fitted on site.
Construction trades.Stonemason: Stonemasons carve and set stone, and the cathedrals of the Middle Ages took generations of them to build.
Construction trades.Drywaller: Drywallers hang plasterboard sheets to form interior walls, a method that replaced slow lath and plaster in the 20th century.
Construction trades.Florist: Florists arrange flowers, and the trade takes skill, but it has no part in building a house.
Construction trades.Barista: Baristas make coffee, and the word is Italian for bartender, so they work in a cafe and not on site.
Construction trades.Cashier: Cashiers handle payments at a till, which is part of a shop, not a building site.
Construction trades.Pharmacist: Pharmacists prepare and advise on medicines, and their training takes years, but it's not a building trade.
Construction trades.Notary: Notaries certify documents and are not tradespeople, even though they may witness a construction contract.
Construction trades.Usher: Ushers show people to seats, which is a job for theatres and weddings, not building.
Construction trades.Sommelier: Sommeliers are wine experts in restaurants, and they're far from a hard hat.
Construction trades.Chiropodist: Chiropodists treat foot problems, and the word comes from Greek for hand and foot, with no building role.
Construction trades.Librarian: Librarians look after books and help people find information, so are on the opposite side of the building trade.
Construction trades.Optician: Opticians fit glasses and lenses, which may need builders to refit the shop, but it's not building work.
Construction trades.Croupier: Croupiers deal casino games, and a casino needs builders to be built, but a croupier isn't one.

Characters from Nintendo games.Mario: Mario first appeared in 1981's Donkey Kong as "Jumpman" and became a plumber later. Nintendo's mascot is one of the best-selling game franchises of all time.
Characters from Nintendo games.Luigi: Luigi is Mario's taller brother, first seen in 1983's Mario Bros. The green-clad sibling later got his own spin-offs, like Luigi's Mansion in 2001.
Characters from Nintendo games.Link: Link is the hero of The Legend of Zelda, though he is not Zelda. Left-handed in most games, he almost never speaks.
Characters from Nintendo games.Zelda: Zelda is the princess, not the hero of her own series. She was named after the writer Zelda Fitzgerald, a fact creator Shigeru Miyamoto has mentioned.
Characters from Nintendo games.Samus: Samus Aran, of Metroid, was a surprise: players learned in 1986 that the armored hero was a woman. It was a big twist for early gaming.
Characters from Nintendo games.Kirby: Kirby first appeared in 1992 on Game Boy, and he can copy enemies' powers by inhaling them. Creator Masahiro Sakurai was only a young developer then.
Characters from Nintendo games.Pikachu: Pikachu became Pokemon's face thanks largely to the anime, which began in 1997. Its name mixes Japanese sounds for a spark (pika) and a mouse squeak (chu).
Characters from Nintendo games.Donkey Kong: Donkey Kong originated in the 1981 arcade game, where he threw barrels at Mario. His name was meant to suggest "stubborn gorilla."
Characters from Nintendo games.Yoshi: Yoshi debuted in 1990's Super Mario World as Mario's dinosaur steed. He can flutter-jump and gobble enemies with a long tongue.
Characters from Nintendo games.Fox McCloud: Fox McCloud is the pilot of Star Fox, which debuted in 1993. The game used a special chip in its cartridge to render 3D graphics on the SNES.
Characters from Nintendo games.Bowser: Bowser is Mario's rival, king of the Koopas, and he has kidnapped Princess Peach over and over since 1985. Japanese fans know him as Koopa.
Characters from Nintendo games.Princess Peach: Peach was called Princess Toadstool in early Western versions. She debuted in 1985 and has led her own game, Super Princess Peach, in 2005.
Characters from Nintendo games.Wario: Wario is Mario's greedy rival, created in 1992. His name combines Mario with the Japanese word warui, which means bad.
Characters from Nintendo games.Sonic: Sonic is a Sega character, created as a rival to Mario in 1991. Not a Nintendo creation, though he later appeared in Nintendo games.
Characters from Nintendo games.Crash Bandicoot: Crash Bandicoot began on the original PlayStation in 1996 as a Sony mascot. He is not from a Nintendo series, though newer games have reached Switch.
Characters from Nintendo games.Lara Croft: Lara Croft is the hero of Tomb Raider, first on Sega Saturn and PlayStation in 1996. She wasn't created by Nintendo.
Characters from Nintendo games.Master Chief: Master Chief is Halo's hero, and Halo is a Microsoft Xbox series that launched in 2001. He is tied to Xbox, not Nintendo.
Characters from Nintendo games.Pac-Man: Pac-Man is a Namco character from 1980. His shape is said to come from a pizza with a slice missing, and he isn't Nintendo's.
Characters from Nintendo games.Mega Man: Mega Man belongs to Capcom, which first released him in 1987. Players may confuse him with Nintendo characters because of the NES era.
Characters from Nintendo games.Spyro: Spyro the Dragon began on PlayStation in 1998. He is an Insomniac and Sony character rather than a Nintendo one.
Characters from Nintendo games.Kratos: Kratos is the Greek-then-Norse god of war from PlayStation's God of War games. He is not a Nintendo character.
Characters from Nintendo games.Solid Snake: Solid Snake is from Konami's Metal Gear series, which started on MSX2 in 1987. Though he appears in Smash Bros., he isn't Nintendo's.
Characters from Nintendo games.Ratchet: Ratchet is a lombax from PlayStation's Ratchet and Clank series, which began in 2002. He doesn't come from Nintendo.
Characters from Nintendo games.Cloud Strife: Cloud Strife is the spiky-haired hero of Final Fantasy VII, a Square game for PlayStation in 1997. He's not a Nintendo character.

Tech that debuted in the 2010s.iPad: Steve Jobs unveiled it in January 2010, and many mocked the name before it sold millions.
Tech that debuted in the 2010s.Instagram: Launched in October 2010, it hit one million users in about two months and sold to Facebook in 2012 for around a billion dollars.
Tech that debuted in the 2010s.Snapchat: Launched in 2011 as Picaboo before a rebrand, it introduced disappearing messages that vanished after viewing.
Tech that debuted in the 2010s.Apple Watch: Released in 2015, it quickly became the most popular smartwatch, and its health and fitness tracking grew into its main selling point.
Tech that debuted in the 2010s.AirPods: Introduced in 2016 alongside the iPhone 7 that removed the headphone jack, and they became a status symbol.
Tech that debuted in the 2010s.Nintendo Switch: Released in 2017, its console-and-handheld design made it one of Nintendo's best-selling machines.
Tech that debuted in the 2010s.Fortnite: Epic's battle royale game launched in 2017 and grew into a global phenomenon with hundreds of millions of players.
Tech that debuted in the 2010s.Alexa: Amazon's voice assistant debuted in 2014 with the Echo speaker, and its name was reportedly inspired by the Library of Alexandria.
Tech that debuted in the 2010s.PS4: Sony's console launched in 2013 and went on to sell more than 100 million units.
Tech that debuted in the 2010s.Pokémon Go: The 2016 augmented-reality game sent millions of people outdoors and passed 500 million downloads within months.
Tech that debuted in the 2010s.Discord: Launched in 2015 as a chat app for gamers, it grew into a general community platform.
Tech that debuted in the 2010s.Tinder: Launched in 2012, it popularized swiping right and left to say yes or no to a stranger's photo.
Tech that debuted in the 2010s.iPhone: Steve Jobs unveiled it in 2007, so it just misses the 2010s.
Tech that debuted in the 2010s.YouTube: The video site was founded in 2005 and first posted a clip called 'Me at the zoo'.
Tech that debuted in the 2010s.Facebook: Mark Zuckerberg started it in 2004 at Harvard, well before the 2010s.
Tech that debuted in the 2010s.Wii: Nintendo's motion-control console was released in 2006 and sold over 100 million units.
Tech that debuted in the 2010s.Kindle: Amazon's e-reader launched in 2007, a few years before the 2010s began.
Tech that debuted in the 2010s.Twitter: Founded in 2006 with 140-character posts, which came from fitting SMS limits.
Tech that debuted in the 2010s.Gmail: Launched on April 1, 2004, it is older than most 2010s tech.
Tech that debuted in the 2010s.Android: Google's mobile OS arrived on phones in 2008, with the HTC Dream as the first.
Tech that debuted in the 2010s.Xbox 360: Microsoft's console launched in 2005 and famously suffered from the 'red ring of death' hardware fault.
Tech that debuted in the 2010s.iPod: Apple's 2001 music player predates the 2010s by almost a decade.
Tech that debuted in the 2010s.Bitcoin: Satoshi Nakamoto's network began in January 2009, so close, yet just before the 2010s.
Tech that debuted in the 2010s.WhatsApp: Launched in 2009, it was already popular before Facebook bought it in 2014.

Members of the Fellowship of the Ring.Frodo: The Ring-bearer, Bilbo's nephew, who carried the One Ring from the Shire to Mount Doom, and wasn't able to destroy it of his own will.
Members of the Fellowship of the Ring.Sam: Frodo's gardener, a humble hobbit, who carries the Ring briefly himself and is, in Tolkien's own view, the story's real hero.
Members of the Fellowship of the Ring.Merry: Short for Meriadoc Brandybuck, Frodo's cousin, who later helps kill the Witch-king alongside Éowyn at the Pelennor Fields.
Members of the Fellowship of the Ring.Pippin: The youngest of the four hobbits, Peregrin Took, who foolishly looks into a palantir and draws Sauron's gaze, but joins Gondor's guard.
Members of the Fellowship of the Ring.Gandalf: The wizard who falls fighting a Balrog in Moria and returns, more powerful, as Gandalf the White.
Members of the Fellowship of the Ring.Aragorn: A Ranger of the North, Isildur's heir, and in the end King Elessar of Gondor, he leads the Fellowship after Gandalf falls.
Members of the Fellowship of the Ring.Legolas: A Sindarin Elf from Mirkwood and a master archer, he is the Fellowship's representative of Elves, as Prince of Mirkwood.
Members of the Fellowship of the Ring.Gimli: The Dwarf from the Lonely Mountain whose friendship with Legolas heals old Elf-Dwarf rivalry; he is the only Dwarf in the company.
Members of the Fellowship of the Ring.Boromir: The Man of Gondor, tempted by the Ring, who tries to take it from Frodo and then dies defending Merry and Pippin.
Members of the Fellowship of the Ring.Bilbo: The Ring's first hobbit finder is not in the Fellowship, as he had left the Ring to Frodo and retired to Rivendell.
Members of the Fellowship of the Ring.Faramir: Boromir's younger brother and a captain of Gondor, he lets Frodo and Sam go instead of seizing the Ring, so he's not in the Fellowship.
Members of the Fellowship of the Ring.Elrond: The half-elven lord of Rivendell, host of the council that formed the Fellowship, but he did not himself join it.
Members of the Fellowship of the Ring.Galadriel: The Lady of Lothlórien gives the Fellowship gifts, like Elven cloaks and the Phial, but stays in her woods.
Members of the Fellowship of the Ring.Gollum: He owned the Ring for about 500 years, and he follows the Fellowship secretly, but not as a member.
Members of the Fellowship of the Ring.Saruman: A wizard who was head of the White Council, he betrays everyone, and thus leads the enemy, not the Fellowship.
Members of the Fellowship of the Ring.Arwen: Elrond's daughter and Aragorn's beloved, who gives up her immortality to marry him; she isn't a Fellowship member.
Members of the Fellowship of the Ring.Éowyn: Rohan's shieldmaiden who kills the Witch-king, ('I am no man'), but she never joined the Fellowship.
Members of the Fellowship of the Ring.Théoden: The King of Rohan, whom Gandalf frees from Saruman's influence, is an ally rather than a Fellowship member.
Members of the Fellowship of the Ring.Treebeard: The oldest Ent, called Fangorn, who sides with the hobbits against Saruman, but is no Fellowship member.
Members of the Fellowship of the Ring.Tom Bombadil: A cheerful, ancient forest-dweller whom the Ring has no power over, he wasn't in the Fellowship and was cut from the films.
Members of the Fellowship of the Ring.Radagast: A wizard of the Istari who lives among animals, he turns up in The Hobbit rather than the Fellowship.
Members of the Fellowship of the Ring.Thorin: The dwarf king of The Hobbit, who led the quest to reclaim Erebor, wasn't in the Fellowship, which came 60 years later.
Members of the Fellowship of the Ring.Bard: The bowman who killed Smaug in The Hobbit is not in the Fellowship, and belongs to an earlier story.
Members of the Fellowship of the Ring.Sauron: The Dark Lord who forged the One Ring is the Fellowship's enemy, not a member.

Characters in Much Ado About Nothing.Beatrice: Her "I had rather hear my dog bark at a crow than a man swear he loves me" sets up her merry war with Benedick.
Characters in Much Ado About Nothing.Benedick: He's tricked into thinking Beatrice loves him by friends who stage an overheard chat, and he soon abandons his vow of bachelorhood.
Characters in Much Ado About Nothing.Hero: Shamed at the altar when Claudio believes she's unfaithful, she's then reported dead and revived.
Characters in Much Ado About Nothing.Claudio: A young count, fooled by a staged window scene, who rejects Hero and must atone by agreeing to marry "her cousin".
Characters in Much Ado About Nothing.Don Pedro: The Prince of Aragon, who plays matchmaker for Beatrice and Benedick, and first woos Hero on Claudio's behalf.
Characters in Much Ado About Nothing.Don John: The Prince's illegitimate brother, an open villain who says "I cannot hide what I am" and sets the whole slander plot moving.
Characters in Much Ado About Nothing.Leonato: The governor of Messina and Hero's father, whose house hosts the returning soldiers. He believes the slander against his daughter.
Characters in Much Ado About Nothing.Dogberry: The pompous constable whose malapropisms ("Comparisons are odorous") do not stop his bumbling watch from catching the real villains.
Characters in Much Ado About Nothing.Borachio: Don John's henchman. His name echoes the Spanish "borracho", drunkard, and he's overheard boasting by the watch.
Characters in Much Ado About Nothing.Margaret: Hero's attendant, who unknowingly takes part in the deception by appearing at Hero's window.
Characters in Much Ado About Nothing.Conrade: Don John's follower, arrested together with Borachio after the watch overhears them boasting about the plot.
Characters in Much Ado About Nothing.Viola: Twelfth Night's heroine, a shipwreck survivor disguised as a boy. She belongs to Illyria, not Messina.
Characters in Much Ado About Nothing.Olivia: A countess in Twelfth Night who ends up chasing a woman in disguise, so she belongs to Illyria, not Messina.
Characters in Much Ado About Nothing.Malvolio: Twelfth Night's steward in yellow stockings. He's the butt of a prank, but in another play.
Characters in Much Ado About Nothing.Rosalind: She flees to the Forest of Arden disguised as a boy in As You Like It, so she belongs to another comedy altogether.
Characters in Much Ado About Nothing.Orlando: The poetic wrestler who falls for Rosalind in As You Like It, a different Shakespeare comedy, and not one set in Messina.
Characters in Much Ado About Nothing.Portia: She's in The Merchant of Venice, and shares a name with Brutus's wife, but she's never in Messina.
Characters in Much Ado About Nothing.Petruchio: The tamer in The Taming of the Shrew, who marries Katherina partly for her dowry. A different battle of the sexes.
Characters in Much Ado About Nothing.Katherina: The shrew in The Taming of the Shrew. Her sharp tongue echoes Beatrice's, but she's from a different play.
Characters in Much Ado About Nothing.Bianca: Katherina's younger sister, besieged by suitors in The Taming of the Shrew, a play set in Padua, not Messina.
Characters in Much Ado About Nothing.Puck: A mischievous sprite who makes the wrong people fall in love in A Midsummer Night's Dream, not in Much Ado.
Characters in Much Ado About Nothing.Oberon: King of the fairies in A Midsummer Night's Dream. A moon of Uranus is also named after him, but he never visits Messina.
Characters in Much Ado About Nothing.Sebastian: Viola's twin in Twelfth Night, and also a name in The Tempest, but he never appears in Much Ado About Nothing.
Characters in Much Ado About Nothing.Juliet: Romeo's love, nearly fourteen in the play, and from Verona. Her tragedy is far from the comedy of Messina.

Characters in As You Like It.Rosalind: The heroine flees into the Forest of Arden disguised as a boy named Ganymede; she has the largest female part in any Shakespeare comedy.
Characters in As You Like It.Celia: Rosalind's cousin and devoted friend goes into exile with her, and takes the name Aliena.
Characters in As You Like It.Orlando: The wrestler-turned-lover hangs love poems for Rosalind on the trees of the forest, and her disguise is the joke.
Characters in As You Like It.Jaques: The melancholy lord delivers the famous 'All the world's a stage' speech about the seven ages of man.
Characters in As You Like It.Touchstone: The court jester follows Celia and Rosalind into exile and wins the country girl Audrey.
Characters in As You Like It.Oliver: Orlando's cruel older brother is transformed by a near-fatal rescue and falls in love with Celia.
Characters in As You Like It.Duke Senior: The rightful duke, exiled by his brother, lives like Robin Hood in the Forest of Arden, and is Rosalind's father.
Characters in As You Like It.Audrey: A simple goatherd who is courted by Touchstone, and she is the play's blunt, earthy counterpoint to the lovers.
Characters in As You Like It.Silvius: A lovesick shepherd who pines after the scornful Phebe, and a stock figure of pastoral romance.
Characters in As You Like It.Phebe: The proud shepherdess scorns Silvius but falls for Rosalind, who is disguised as a boy.
Characters in As You Like It.Adam: The loyal old servant who follows Orlando into exile is traditionally said to have been played by Shakespeare himself.
Characters in As You Like It.Corin: The old shepherd who gives the exiles a cottage and good country advice about the value of simple life.
Characters in As You Like It.Viola: Viola is the cross-dressing heroine of Twelfth Night, though Rosalind has a similar disguise in this play.
Characters in As You Like It.Olivia: Olivia is the countess in Twelfth Night, who falls for the disguised Viola.
Characters in As You Like It.Beatrice: Beatrice trades barbs with Benedick in Much Ado About Nothing.
Characters in As You Like It.Hero: Hero is the wronged bride in Much Ado About Nothing.
Characters in As You Like It.Hermia: Hermia is one of the runaway lovers in A Midsummer Night's Dream.
Characters in As You Like It.Helena: Helena chases Demetrius through the woods in A Midsummer Night's Dream; the name also appears in All's Well That Ends Well.
Characters in As You Like It.Miranda: Prospero's daughter lives on an island in The Tempest.
Characters in As You Like It.Perdita: Perdita is the lost princess raised by shepherds in The Winter's Tale.
Characters in As You Like It.Imogen: Imogen is the heroine of Cymbeline, who also disguises herself as a boy.
Characters in As You Like It.Portia: Portia disguises herself as a lawyer in The Merchant of Venice, which is a different play.
Characters in As You Like It.Kate: Kate is the 'shrew' of The Taming of the Shrew.
Characters in As You Like It.Bianca: Bianca is Kate's sister in The Taming of the Shrew.

Things that are usually white.Salt: Table salt is sodium chloride, and its crystals are cubes, which are clear but look white when crushed.

Things that are usually white.Cotton ball: Cotton is nearly pure cellulose, and it is naturally white or cream.

Things that are usually white.Pearl: Pearls form when an oyster coats an irritant in layers of nacre, and they can also be pink, gold or black.
Things that are usually white.Snowman: Snowmen date back centuries, and the earliest known picture of one is from 1380 in a manuscript.
Things that are usually white.Chalk: Blackboard chalk is now often gypsum, while natural chalk is limestone made from tiny ancient sea creatures.
Things that are usually white.Banana: Bananas are yellow, and they're slightly radioactive from the potassium inside them.
Things that are usually white.Lemon: Lemons are yellow, and they're acidic enough to clean copper pans.
Things that are usually white.Fire truck: It's typically red, though in some countries they are lime-yellow.
Things that are usually white.Grass: Grass is green because it has chlorophyll, and it is a plant family with thousands of species.
Things that are usually white.Carrot: Carrots are orange, thanks to beta carotene, but purple and white ones exist.
Things that are usually white.Crow: Crows are black, and they are intelligent birds that can recognise human faces.
Things that are usually white.Coal: Coal is black, and it is made from ancient plants compressed over millions of years.
Things that are usually white.Chocolate: Chocolate is brown, and white chocolate has no cocoa solids, only cocoa butter.
Things that are usually white.Coffee: Coffee is brown from roasting the beans, and beans start off green.
Things that are usually white.Tomato: Tomatoes are red, and were once feared as poisonous in parts of Europe.
Things that are usually white.Ketchup: Ketchup is red because of tomatoes, so it is no white condiment.
Things that are usually white.Blueberry: Blueberries are blue thanks to a waxy bloom, which is a surprise since their flesh is greenish.

Colors named after foods.Vermilion: Vermilion is a bright red-orange named for a mineral pigment, cinnabar, not food.

Things that have a cockpit.Glider: Glider pilots sit in a small cockpit, where they fly without an engine, relying on rising air.

Things that have a cockpit.Racing yacht: Racing yachts have cockpits where crew sit, and the crew pull winches there to trim the sails.
Things that have a cockpit.Biplane: Biplane pilots often sat in open cockpits, wearing goggles and scarves to keep out the wind.

Things that have a cockpit.Skateboard: A skateboard has no cockpit; the rider just stands on the deck.

Tire brands.Michelin: Brothers André and Édouard Michelin founded it in 1889, and the tire company later created the famous restaurant guide to get drivers on the road.
Tire brands.Goodyear: The company is named after Charles Goodyear, who discovered vulcanized rubber in 1839, though he never worked for it.
Tire brands.Pirelli: An Italian brand founded in 1872, Pirelli is the sole tire supplier to Formula One today and publishes the famed Pirelli Calendar.
Tire brands.Bridgestone: Founded in Japan in 1931, its name is a translation of the founder's surname, Ishibashi, meaning 'stone bridge'.
Tire brands.Dunlop: John Boyd Dunlop invented the pneumatic tire in 1888 to give his young son's tricycle a smoother ride.
Tire brands.Continental: A German company founded in Hanover in 1871, it began making rubber goods before turning to car and bicycle tires.
Tire brands.Firestone: Founded by Harvey Firestone in 1900, the brand supplied tires for Henry Ford's cars and for the Indianapolis 500.
Tire brands.Yokohama: A Japanese tire maker named for its port hometown, Yokohama began in 1917 as a joint venture with B.F. Goodrich.
Tire brands.Hankook: A South Korean tire company founded in 1941, its name means 'Korea' in Korean.
Tire brands.Toyo: A Japanese tire brand known for off-road tires; its name simply means 'Orient' or 'East'.
Tire brands.Shell: A trap: Shell is an oil and fuel company, with a seashell logo, rather than a tire maker.
Tire brands.Castrol: Castrol makes motor oil, not tires, and its name comes from the castor oil used in early engine lubricants.
Tire brands.Bosch: The German firm Bosch makes spark plugs, brakes and electronics, but not tires.
Tire brands.Exxon: Exxon is an oil company; the name was invented in 1972 as a new brand for Standard Oil of New Jersey.
Tire brands.BP: BP is a petroleum company that began as the Anglo-Persian Oil Company in 1909.
Tire brands.Mobil: Mobil is a fuel and oil brand with a famous red Pegasus logo, and is now part of ExxonMobil.
Tire brands.Valvoline: Valvoline, founded in 1866, is among the oldest motor oil brands, but it doesn't make tires.
Tire brands.AutoZone: AutoZone is a US auto parts retailer; it sells tires made by others instead of producing them.
Tire brands.Garmin: Garmin is a navigation and wearables company; its name combines the founders' first names Gary Burrell and Min Kao.
Tire brands.TomTom: TomTom is a Dutch maker of satnavs and map data, not tires.
Tire brands.Brembo: Brembo is an Italian brand famous for brake discs and calipers, and not for rubber on the road.
Tire brands.Recaro: Recaro is a German maker of racing and car seats, not tires.
Tire brands.Texaco: Texaco, with its red star logo, is a fuel brand; the name stands for 'Texas Company'.
Tire brands.Halfords: Halfords is a British retailer of car and bike parts; it sells tires but doesn't make them.

Things worn around the neck.Scarf: Scarves go back to ancient China, where terracotta army soldiers wore neck cloths. Some regiments even used them as rank markers.
Things worn around the neck.Necklace: Shell bead necklaces found in Africa and the Middle East are about 75,000 years old, perhaps humanity's oldest jewelry.
Things worn around the neck.Tie: The necktie descends from Croatian mercenaries' scarves in the 1600s, which French court fashion took up as a 'cravate'.
Things worn around the neck.Bow tie: Bow ties began as a practical way for soldiers to tie off shirt collars. Today most are pre-tied clips, though classic ones are hand-tied.
Things worn around the neck.Choker: A choker is a tight necklace. Victorian ladies wore velvet chokers, and they returned in the 1990s.
Things worn around the neck.Cravat: The cravat takes its name from 'Croat'. Louis XIV loved the Croatian soldiers' neckcloths and made them court fashion.
Things worn around the neck.Lanyard: A lanyard is a cord for ID badges or keys. The word comes from French 'laniere', a strap, and originally referred to a sailor's rope.
Things worn around the neck.Locket: A locket opens to hold a photo or lock of hair, and Victorians wore them to remember loved ones.
Things worn around the neck.Pendant: A pendant hangs from a chain around the neck. The word comes from Latin for 'hanging', and some cultures wear them as amulets.
Things worn around the neck.Ascot: The ascot tie is named after the Royal Ascot horse races in England, where gentlemen once wore the wide silk neckwear.
Things worn around the neck.Neckerchief: A neckerchief is a small cloth knotted around the neck. Scouts and cowboys wear them, and the bandana is a close cousin.
Things worn around the neck.Lei: A lei is a Hawaiian garland of flowers, shells or feathers. Giving one is a sign of aloha, and refusing it is considered rude.
Things worn around the neck.Feather boa: A feather boa is a fluffy scarf of feathers worn around the neck. It was popular with flappers and burlesque stars.
Things worn around the neck.Belt: A belt goes around the waist, not the neck. Wrestling champions have worn championship belts as trophies since the 1800s.
Things worn around the neck.Anklet: An anklet circles the ankle, not the neck. Anklets are common in India, where they often carry tiny bells.
Things worn around the neck.Bracelet: A bracelet circles the wrist. Ancient Egyptians wore them, and some were buried with pharaohs.
Things worn around the neck.Cufflink: Cufflinks fasten the cuffs of a dress shirt at the wrist. They became fashionable once French-cuff shirts arrived.
Things worn around the neck.Wristwatch: A wristwatch sits on the wrist. The first ones were women's jewelry, and soldiers made them popular in the First World War.
Things worn around the neck.Earring: Earrings hang from the earlobe. Ötzi the Iceman, over 5,000 years old, had stretched lobes that held ornaments.
Things worn around the neck.Sock: Socks cover the feet. The word comes from the Latin 'soccus', a light slipper worn by Roman actors.
Things worn around the neck.Tiara: A tiara sits on top of the head, not the neck, and is worn by royals and brides on special occasions.
Things worn around the neck.Garter: A garter holds up a stocking on the leg. Bridal garter tossing is an old wedding custom, much like the bouquet.
Things worn around the neck.Toe ring: A toe ring is worn on a toe, not the neck. In India, silver toe rings are a traditional sign that a woman is married.
Things worn around the neck.Mitten: A mitten covers the hand with one thumb pocket. They keep fingers warmer than gloves because the fingers share heat.

Things worn for swimming or surfing.Speedos: The brand name came from a 1928 slogan encouraging Australians to 'Speed on in your Speedos', and the name later became general for tight trunks.
Things worn for swimming or surfing.Tankini: This two-piece pairs a tank-style top with bottoms, so it gives more midriff cover than a bikini and is easy to swim in.
Things worn for swimming or surfing.Wetsuit: Neoprene suits do not stay dry: a thin layer of water trapped against your skin warms up and acts as insulation.
Things worn for swimming or surfing.Boardshorts: Long, loose boardshorts took over from tight woolen trunks in surf culture, and they are made to dry quickly between waves.
Things worn for swimming or surfing.Swim trunks: Roomier than briefs, trunks sit mid-thigh and are the everyday men's swimwear in much of the world.
Things worn for swimming or surfing.Burkini: Created by Aheda Zanetti in Australia in 2003, its name blends burqa and bikini, and it covers body and head except for the face.
Things worn for swimming or surfing.Monokini: This one-piece with no top was designed by Rudi Gernreich in 1964, as a statement about freedom, and it caused a major stir.
Things worn for swimming or surfing.Rash guard: This snug stretchy shirt guards against chafing from wetsuits and surfboards, and it blocks sunburn on long days in the sun.
Things worn for swimming or surfing.Swimsuit: Swimsuit is the plain catch-all, and it is a surprising modern idea: laws once banned bathing in anything revealing in many countries.
Things worn for swimming or surfing.Leotard: It is named after Jules Leotard, a French trapeze artist who invented the flying trapeze act, and it is for gym and dance, not water.
Things worn for swimming or surfing.Tutu: Tutus are layered tulle dance skirts, and wet netting would drag a swimmer down and look a mess.
Things worn for swimming or surfing.Pajamas: The word comes from Hindi and Urdu for loose trousers, and pajamas are made for bed, not water.
Things worn for swimming or surfing.Kimono: Kimono means a thing to wear in Japanese, and the silk robe is wrapped left over right, which would be a mess in the surf.
Things worn for swimming or surfing.Corset: Boning and laces cinch the waist, so a corset would be hard to breathe in, let alone swim in.
Things worn for swimming or surfing.Tracksuit: Tracksuits became fashion in the 1980s through hip-hop, but the polyester ones do not suit swimming.
Things worn for swimming or surfing.Overalls: Overalls are bib-and-strap workwear, and their heavy denim would soak up water and sink you.
Things worn for swimming or surfing.Tuxedo: A tuxedo is formalwear named after Tuxedo Park in New York, and it would be a dire choice for the beach.
Things worn for swimming or surfing.Raincoat: A raincoat is made to shed water and keep you dry, which is the reverse of what swimming demands.
Things worn for swimming or surfing.Lab coat: The white lab coat signals cleanliness in science and medicine, and is not for swimming.
Things worn for swimming or surfing.Poncho: The poncho is a South American cloak that sheds rain on land, and it is no match for waves.
Things worn for swimming or surfing.Onesie: Onesies are one-piece cosy loungewear that, once wet, would be heavy and hard to swim in.
Things worn for swimming or surfing.Cardigan: Wool is named for the Earl of Cardigan, and a wet wool cardigan is heavy as a rock and offers no help in water.
Things worn for swimming or surfing.Kilt: A kilt is heavy pleated tartan wool, and drenched in a lake it would take ages to dry.

Words for a fool (not a clever person).Dunce: It comes from the followers of medieval scholar Duns Scotus, whose ideas fell out of favour, turning his disciples' name into an insult.

Words for a fool (not a clever person).Dolt: It probably relates to the old word dulled, meaning blunted. It has been used for a stupid person since the 1500s.
Words for a fool (not a clever person).Numbskull: This is a mix of numb and skull, an insult for someone whose head seems too dulled to think. It is often also spelled numskull.
Words for a fool (not a clever person).Ninny: It may be a shortening of innocent, and it was used in Shakespeare's time. It is a gentle insult, never a vicious one.
Words for a fool (not a clever person).Chump: Originally it meant a short, thick lump of wood, and the idea of a blockhead followed from that. A chump change is a trivial amount.
Words for a fool (not a clever person).Clod: A clod is a lump of earth, so a person called one is thought to be heavy-headed and clumsy, as if made of dirt.
Words for a fool (not a clever person).Twit: It once meant to tease, and the noun came later. Today it is a mild British insult, as in the title of Roald Dahl's The Twits.
Words for a fool (not a clever person).Oaf: It comes from an Old Norse word for an elf, and a changeling left by elves was thought to be a clumsy, dim child.
Words for a fool (not a clever person).Imbecile: It was once a formal medical term for a level of intellectual disability, and it later became a general insult, which many now avoid.
Words for a fool (not a clever person).Sage: It does not belong, because a sage is wise. The word also names a herb whose Latin name, salvia, means to heal.
Words for a fool (not a clever person).Scholar: This is a person of learning, so not a fool. The word comes from Latin schola, meaning school, which is the same root as the word school.
Words for a fool (not a clever person).Genius: It is the opposite of a fool. In ancient Rome, a genius was a guardian spirit that each person was thought to be born with.
Words for a fool (not a clever person).Mastermind: It names a brilliant planner and so isn't a fool. It is also a famous quiz show, which has run in Britain since 1972.
Words for a fool (not a clever person).Savant: It means a learned person, from French for knowing. The term savant syndrome describes people with remarkable skills in a narrow field.
Words for a fool (not a clever person).Whiz: Short for wizard, it means someone really skilled. A whiz kid is a young person who succeeds spectacularly early.
Words for a fool (not a clever person).Egghead: It is a term for an intellectual, which was often used with slight mockery since the 1920s, and a bald head was one image behind it.
Words for a fool (not a clever person).Pundit: It comes from the Hindi word pandit, a learned scholar, and it now means an expert who gives opinions, usually in the media.
Words for a fool (not a clever person).Prodigy: It names a child with extraordinary talent. Mozart, composing before the age of six, is the classic example.
Words for a fool (not a clever person).Brainiac: The word comes from a villain in Superman comics who first appeared in 1958, and it became a name for a very smart person.
Words for a fool (not a clever person).Boffin: British slang for a scientific expert, it was popularised in World War II for the radar and code researchers behind the scenes.
Words for a fool (not a clever person).Polymath: It describes someone skilled in many fields, such as Leonardo da Vinci, from Greek words meaning much learning.
